text: What does `@Override` do that the compiler would not do without it?
choices: It permits a subclass method to narrow the access of the method it replaces.
It makes the compiler reject the method if it does not actually replace an inherited one.
It generates the `super` call automatically at the start of the method body.
It forces the method to be dispatched dynamically rather than statically.
explanation: It converts a silent mistake into a compile error. Chapter 20's `equals(Point o)` is the standard case: the parameter type is wrong, so it is an overload rather than an override, the collections keep calling the inherited `Object.equals`, and nothing reports it. With `@Override` present the code does not compile.
